beats.say: In 1911 the Ottoman navy secretly commissioned a fleet of German-built submarines, unseen by rivals.
These U-boats, named after mythic sea monsters, aimed to protect the dwindling Ottoman coastlines in the Aegean.
Sultan Mehmed V approved the project on March 12, fearing Greek insurgents could seize Crete by summer.
German engineer Arthur Krupp negotiated a covert deal at the Istanbul railway station, exchanging torpedoes for silk.
beats.visual: Arthur Krupp Istanbul railway station meeting 1911

beats.say: The first submarine, Abdülhamid, slipped beneath the Bosphorus on June 5, testing its silent glide.
British intelligence caught wind, but dismissed it as Ottoman theatrics, unaware of the looming Dardanelles trap.
By September the fleet patrolled the Aegean, deterring Greek smuggling ships that fed the Macedonian rebels.
beats.visual: Aegean Sea patrol Ottoman submarines 1911 map

beats.say: When the First Balkan War erupted, the hidden submarines torpedoed an Italian cruiser near Salonika, shocking Europe.
The Ottoman press hailed the victory, yet the empire soon faced internal revolt after the 1912 Young Turk coup.
History forgets this naval surge, but it proved the empire could still strike fear beneath the waves.
